anomaly_def.Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Database Memory Allocation Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Composite definition: The database simultaneously suffers from excessive accumulation of obsolete MVCC row versions and uncontrolled growth of memory-resident structures, causing both storage-level bloat and host-level memory pressure at the same time.

MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly: Obsolete row versions, undo/rollback records, and dead index entries pile up faster than background cleanup processes can purge them, inflating on-disk objects and lengthening visibility checks.
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly: Buffer caches, work areas, plan caches, and other memory heaps expand beyond the safe limits of physical RAM, leading to paging, OOM kills, and degraded cache efficiency.

Combined symptoms: • Rapid growth of both on-disk relation size and in-memory buffers devoted to stale row versions and undo, driving the database process’s RSS steadily upward. • Cleanup workers that are chronically scheduled yet starved for RAM, showing frequent restarts or throttling under OS memory pressure. • Elevated I/O due to double handling of data: bloated tables require longer scans while reduced cache effectiveness forces more disk reads; simultaneous swapping further slows I/O paths. • Query latencies become highly variable: readers traverse ever-larger version chains while also stalling on memory allocation, and writers may experience checkpoint or WAL backpressure. • Nodes in clustered/VM environments may be evicted or reboot due to exceeded memory cgroups, with recovery complicated by large undo/redo segments.

Causal interaction: The surge of obsolete versions expands both the persistent heap and the in-memory buffer pool, directly increasing memory consumption. As the memory envelope is exceeded, the operating system begins paging or terminates processes, which in turn slows or interrupts background vacuum/garbage-collection workers, allowing even more dead versions to accumulate—a positive feedback loop. Memory pressure also reduces effective work memory per query, causing hash/sort spills that further inflate temporary files and prolong transactions, keeping old snapshots open and preventing version pruning. Conversely, long-running or memory-hungry queries spawned during memory bloat delay transaction-ID advancement, deepening the MVCC horizon problem. The intertwined effects amplify each other, degrading throughput, increasing crash risk, and making root-cause isolation harder because symptoms of storage bloat and memory exhaustion appear concurrently.

entry.official_definition: The length of time in seconds an InnoDB transaction waits for a row lock before giving up.
entry.trigger_condition: An InnoDB transaction waits longer than innodb_lock_wait_timeout for a row lock.
entry.workload_impact: The lock wait gives up; by default only the current statement is rolled back unless innodb_rollback_on_timeout is enabled.
entry.default_behavior: Defined as an InnoDB system variable.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when a statement cannot obtain the required lock within the configured waiting window because another transaction or metadata operation is holding an incompatible lock.
entry.solution_guidance: Inspect blocking sessions, reduce conflicting transaction overlap, shorten transaction lifetime, and review lock scheduling and schema-change timing.
